# Multiplexer

> A lightweight, highly available message broker for request/reply and publish/subscribe messaging between microservices on a trusted internal network: peers connect over TCP, announce a peer type, and exchange typed messages routed by a declarative rules file, with round-robin load balancing, fan-out and automatic failover across active-active instances. Stateless, no single point of failure. C++17 core, C++ and Python client libraries, built with Bazel.

Vocabulary used everywhere: a peer is a client (passive, sends requests or events) or a backend (runs the library loop, receives, may answer); both talk to multiplexers.

## Facts to know before reading further

- Prerequisites: Bazel 6.2.1 through Bazelisk (`.bazelversion`), a C++17 compiler (gcc 11 or newer, clang 18), `protoc` with `libprotobuf` of the same version, Python 3.10 or newer with headers and `python3-protobuf`; Boost, pybind11 and googletest are fetched by Bazel. Verified on clean Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 (docs/building.md).
- Consuming it: declare the repository as `@mx` with `git_repository`, call `mx_dependencies()` then `mx_setup()` in WORKSPACE, point the build at your rules file with `--@mx//:multiplexer_rules=`, depend on `@mx//multiplexer:clients` or `:servers` (Python) and `@mx//multiplexer:client` (C++); tests get `@mx//multiplexer/testing`.
- Guarantees: a message is delivered at most once per multiplexer to whoever is connected now, nothing is queued or persisted; a request whose reply is late is sent again to another backend, so a backend may receive a request twice and every attempt has a new id; no authentication, for a trusted network (docs/guarantees.md).
- Reserved: peer types and message types 1 to 99 belong to the protocol; deployments use 100 and up in their own rules file, from which the constants are generated (docs/rules.md).
